To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the performance of HetNets with correlated user and base station locations is significantly different than the case where these locations are assumed to be independent.

the coverage probability of a typical user decreases as the frequency reuse increases and the number of SSBs per user hotspot increases, and the average throughput of the user increases as the frequency reuse and the number of users per hotspot increase.

(1) power-based association provides higher coverage probability and throughput than the distance-based association, (2) the distance-based association is more robust to correlation between the locations of user hotspots and their associated SBSs, and (3) the distance-based and power-based associations provide the same coverage probability when the locations of users are independent of the locations of SBSs.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we provide a comprehensive analysis of HetNet performance in the presence of correlation between user and SBS locations, which is the key to the accurate modeling and analysis of future HetNets with SBSs deployed at user hotspots.
we have developed a new analytical model for HetNets that can capture correlation between the locations of the users and their serving small cell base stations.
our results can be used by the network operators to determine the optimal number of SBS reusing the same frequency resource block, which would provide the best coverage probability and throughput.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the proposed model and the derived results provide a comprehensive analysis tool to understand the performance of HetNets in a wide range of practical scenarios.
the performance of a HetNet is strongly influenced by the correlation in the user and SBS locations and that ignoring this correlation may lead to erroneous performance evaluation.
